...${...}....returns: `str` — the pieces with the values in place.

params: optional: the value the loop takes
break.returns: it never returns: the loop ends here.
examples:
// it works in map, filter and reduce too
list.map(l, if(_ < 0, break(), _ * 2));

c_for.doc: The loop of C: an initialisation, a condition, a step, and a body.
c_for.returns: the value of the last round.
examples: c_for(i = size(l) - 1, i >= 0, i -= 1, print(l:i));   // backwards

call.doc: Calls a function held in a value, with those arguments.
params: the function, as a value or as a name
examples:
// calling every function of a list
for(handlers, call(_, event));
call.note: Calling a function held in a variable directly (`handler(21)`) also works; `call` is for when the function arrives as a value from somewhere else.

concat.doc: The pieces of an interpolated string, already separated by the tokenizer.
concat.returns: `str` — the pieces one after the other.

continue.doc: Skips to the next round of the innermost loop.
params: optional: the value of this round
continue.returns: it never returns: this round ends here.

exit.doc: Stops the whole script, not just the current function.
params: optional: the value of the script
exit.returns: it never returns: everything ends here.
examples: if(!entity.player(), exit('this script needs a player'));

fn.doc: A function written without a name.
params: the parameters, optionally typed, as in a declaration

for.doc: Runs an expression once for every element of a list.
params: computed for every element: `_` is the element, `_i` its index
for.returns: `num` — how many times the expression came out true.
examples:
// counting: it returns the number of true results
found = for(positions, block.block(_) == 'diamond_ore');

if.doc: Chooses between expressions. With more pairs it is a chain of cases, and the odd last argument is the fallback.
params: computed when the condition is true
computed when none of the conditions is true
if.returns: the value of the branch that ran, `null` when none did.
if.note: Only the branch that is chosen is computed: the others are never touched.

loop.doc: Repeats an expression a fixed number of times.
params: the body; `_` is the number of the round, from zero
loop.returns: the value of the last round.
loop.note: It is the cheapest of the loops: it allocates no list, unlike `for(range(n), ...)`.

match.doc: Picks a branch by the shape of a value.
match.returns: `any` — the result of the arm that matched, `null` when none did.

not.doc: The truth value turned round - the same thing the `!` operator does.
not.returns: `bool` — `true` when the value counted as false.
examples: not([]);       // true: an empty list counts as false
!condition;    // the usual way to write it

outer.doc: Captures a variable of the enclosing scope inside a function, by value.
params: the name of the variable to capture
examples:
limit = 10;
fn check(x, outer(limit)) -> x < limit;
outer.note: It goes among the parameters of the function and captures **the value it has at that moment**: later changes to the outer variable are not seen.

print.doc: Writes a message to whoever launched the script, or to a given target.
params: optional: a player, or a list of players
what to write; formatted text works too
print.returns: the message, so the call can be slipped in the middle of an expression.
examples:
// it returns its argument: handy while debugging
result = compute(print(input));

return.doc: Leaves the current function at once, with a value.
params: what the function gives back; without it, `null`
return.returns: it never returns: the function ends here.
return.note: The last expression of a function is already its value: `return` is for leaving early, in the middle of a loop or after a check.

throw.doc: Raises an error that a `try` further up can catch.
params: optional: the name of the kind of error; without it, `'user_exception'`
what to hand to the catcher, where it arrives as `_`
throw.returns: it never returns: it unwinds to the nearest `try`.

try.doc: Runs an expression and catches the errors it raises.
params: the kind of error to catch: `'value_exception'`, `'io_exception'`, `'json_error'`, `'nbt_error'`, `'user_exception'`, `'unknown_block'`, ...
computed when the error was caught: `_` is the value thrown, `_trace` the stack
try.returns: the value of the expression, or the one of the branch that caught the error.
examples:
// _ holds what was thrown
try(throw('too many'), print('failed: ' + _));
try.note: With no type it only catches what a script threw with `throw`, not the errors of the language: an error in your own code stays visible instead of being swallowed.

while.doc: Repeats an expression as long as the condition holds.
params: optional: the maximum number of rounds
the body; `_` is the number of the round
while.returns: the value of the last round.
examples:
// with a ceiling, so a wrong condition does not hang the server
while(!done, 1000, step());

abs.doc: The absolute value of a number: the distance from zero, always positive.

acos.doc: The arc cosine: the angle whose cosine is `x`.
acos.returns: `num` — the angle in radians, from `0` to `pi`.

acosh.returns: `num` — the argument that produces it, not negative.

acot.doc: The arc cotangent: the angle whose cotangent is `x`.

asin.doc: The arc sine: the angle whose sine is `x`.
asin.returns: `num` — the angle in radians, from `-pi/2` to `pi/2`.

atan.doc: The arc tangent: the angle whose tangent is `x`.
atan.returns: `num` — the angle in radians, from `-pi/2` to `pi/2`.

atan2.doc: The angle of the point `(x, y)` measured from the positive x axis, with the right quadrant.
atan2.returns: `num` — the angle in radians, from `-pi` to `pi`.
examples:
// the yaw pointing from one position to another
math.deg(math.atan2(z2 - z1, x2 - x1)) - 90;
atan2.note: The one to use for directions: `atan(y / x)` cannot tell apart two opposite points and divides by zero on the vertical.

bitwise_and.doc: The bit by bit `and` of two whole numbers: a bit survives only where both have it.
params: the whole numbers, or a single list of them

bitwise_arithmetic_shift_right.doc: Shifts the bits to the right keeping the sign - a division by a power of two, rounded downwards.

bitwise_not.doc: Flips every bit of a whole number.
bitwise_not.returns: `num` — `-n - 1`, which is what flipping every bit means in two's complement.

bitwise_or.doc: The bit by bit `or`: a bit survives where at least one of the two has it.
params: the whole numbers, or a single list of them
examples:
// turning a flag on
flags = math.bitwise_or(flags, 4);

bitwise_popcount.doc: How many bits of a whole number are set to one.
bitwise_popcount.returns: `num` — the count of the bits at one.

bitwise_roll_left.doc: Rotates the bits to the left: what leaves on one side comes back on the other.

bitwise_roll_right.doc: Rotates the bits to the right: what leaves on one side comes back on the other.

bitwise_shift_left.doc: Shifts the bits to the left, filling with zeros - a multiplication by a power of two.

bitwise_shift_right.doc: Shifts the bits to the right filling with zeros, the sign included.
bitwise_shift_right.returns: `num` — the shifted value, always not negative.
examples: math.bitwise_shift_right(-1, 60);  // 15: the sign bit is shifted too

bitwise_xor.doc: The bit by bit exclusive `or`: a bit survives where exactly one of the two has it.
params: the whole numbers, or a single list of them

ceil.doc: The smallest whole number that is not smaller than `x`.

cos.doc: The cosine of an angle in radians.
examples:
// a circle of radius 5 around the origin
for(range(360), block.set([math.cos(math.rad(_)) * 5, 64, math.sin(math.rad(_)) * 5], 'stone'));

cosh.doc: The hyperbolic cosine, `(e^x + e^-x) / 2` - the shape of a hanging chain.

double_to_long_bits.doc: The bits of a decimal number read as a whole number, without converting the value.
double_to_long_bits.returns: `num` — the same 64 bits, read as a whole number.
double_to_long_bits.note: It is the pair of `long_to_double_bits`: they go back and forth over the same bits, and are how you hash or serialise a decimal without losing a digit.

fact.doc: The factorial of a whole number: `n * (n-1) * ... * 1`.
params: a whole number that is not negative

floor.doc: The largest whole number that is not greater than `x`.
floor.note: It is the one to use to turn a position into block coordinates: `floor(-0.3)` is `-1`, which is the block you are standing in, while `round` would give `0`.

ln1p.doc: The natural logarithm of `1 + x`, accurate for very small `x`.
ln1p.note: `ln(1 + x)` loses every significant digit when `x` is tiny, because `1 + x` is already `1`. This one does not.

log1p.doc: The logarithm in base 10 of `1 + x`, accurate for very small `x`.

long_to_double_bits.doc: The bits of a whole number read as a decimal number, without converting the value.
long_to_double_bits.returns: `num` — the same 64 bits, read as a decimal.

mandelbrot.doc: How many iterations the point `(x, y)` survives before the Mandelbrot sequence diverges.
mandelbrot.returns: `num` — the iterations reached; the limit means the point is inside the set.

max.doc: The largest of the arguments, or of the elements of a single list.
params: two or more values, or one list

min.doc: The smallest of the arguments, or of the elements of a single list.
params: two or more values, or one list

number.doc: Converts a value to a number.
params: the value to convert, usually a string
number.returns: `num` — the value read as a number.
number.note: A value that is not a number raises a `TypeMismatchError` with the position of the call: it does not come back as `null` to be discovered three lines further down.

perlin.doc: Samples Perlin noise: a value that changes smoothly with the coordinates, the same at the same point.
params: the point to sample; the missing coordinates count as zero
optional: a different seed gives a different landscape
perlin.note: The scale is in the coordinates you pass: dividing them makes the features wider, multiplying makes them noisier.

rad.doc: Converts degrees into radians - what every trigonometric function here wants.

rand.doc: A random number between zero and the limit, or a random element when the argument is a list.
params: a number (upper bound, excluded) or a list to pick from
optional: draws from a generator bound to that seed instead of the shared one
rand.returns: `num` when the limit is a number, otherwise one element of the list.
examples: floor(math.rand(10));               // a whole number from 0 to 9
rand.note: The result is a decimal number: `rand(10)` is not a whole number, put a `floor` around it when you want one.

relu.doc: The number itself when positive, zero otherwise - the rectifier of neural networks.

reset_seed.doc: Restarts the random generator bound to a seed, so the same sequence of draws comes out again.
params: the name of the generator, a number or a string
reset_seed.returns: `num` — how many draws that generator had made before being reset.
examples:
math.reset_seed('test');
math.rand(100, 'test');   // always the same value after a reset
reset_seed.note: It is what makes a test on random code repeatable: reset, run, compare.

round.doc: Rounds to the nearest whole number, halves going away from zero.

sign.doc: The sign of a number, as -1, 0 or 1.
sign.returns: `num` — `-1` when negative, `0` when zero, `1` when positive.

simplex.doc: Samples simplex noise: like `perlin`, with fewer directional artefacts.
params: optional: the seed of the noise

sin.doc: The sine of an angle in radians.

params: a number that is not negative
examples:
// distance between two points
math.sqrt((x2 - x1) ^ 2 + (z2 - z1) ^ 2);

tan.doc: The tangent of an angle in radians.

tanh.doc: The hyperbolic tangent: squashes any number into the range -1 to 1.

decode_base64.doc: Reads back a string encoded in base64.

hash_code.doc: A stable numeric hash of any value, lists and maps included.
hash_code.returns: `num` — the hash; equal values give equal hashes.
examples:
// choosing a colour from a name, always the same one
palette:(abs(string.hash_code(name)) % size(palette));
hash_code.note: It is a hash, not an identifier: two different values can collide. It is fine for a bucket or a colour, not to tell one thing from another.

examples:
// comparing names without caring about case
if(string.lower(typed) == string.lower(expected), 'the same');

replace.doc: Replaces every part of the string matching a regular expression.
params: what to put in its place
optional: how many occurrences, all of them when absent
replace.returns: `str` — the string with every occurrence replaced.
replace.note: The pattern is a regular expression, not a plain piece of text: `.`, `*`, `+`, `(`, `[` have a meaning and have to be escaped with `\\` to be searched literally.

split.doc: The inverse of `join`: cuts a string into a list of pieces.
params: the pattern where to cut, a regular expression

str.doc: Builds a string. With one argument it is the textual form of the value; with more, `format` is a template filled with the ones that follow.
params: the value, or the template: `%s` a value, `%d` a whole number, `%.2f` a decimal with two digits, `%%` a literal percent
what fills the placeholders, in order; a single list is spread over them
examples: string.str('%s has %d points', name, 12);     // 'ada has 12 points'
str.note: It is the readable way to build a message: `'x: ' + x + ', y: ' + y` grows one concatenation per value, `str('x: %d, y: %d', x, y)` stays one line.

title.doc: The string with the find letter of every word in upper case and the rest in lower case.
examples:
// from the id of a block to a readable name
string.title(string.replace('minecraft:oak_stairs', '.*:|_', ' '));

all.doc: Whether every element satisfies the condition.
params: computed for every element: `_` is the element, `_i` its index
examples: list.all(positions, block.air(_));       // whether the space is free

filter.doc: The elements that satisfy a condition, in the same order.
params: computed for every element: `_` is the element, `_i` its index
filter.returns: `list` — the elements for which the condition came out true.

find.doc: The find element that satisfies the condition, `null` when none does.
params: computed for every element: `_` is the element, `_i` its index
find.note: It stops at the find hit: on a long list it is not `filter(...):0`, which would walk over all of it.

get.doc: The element at that index, the same thing the `:` operator does.
params: the position, from zero; negative counts from the end
get.note: Reading **wraps around**: index `3` on a list of three elements comes back to the find one. It is deleting that refuses an index that does not exist.

has.doc: Whether **that index** exists in the list - not whether the list contains a value.
has.returns: `bool` — whether the index is inside the list.
examples:
// membership is a different question
([1, 2, 3] ~ 2) != null;     // true: `~` gives the index, or null

join.doc: Joins values into a single string, putting the separator between them.
params: the text to insert between the pieces
the list to join, or the values one by one

map.doc: Applies an expression to every element and collects the results.
params: computed for every element: `_` is the element, `_i` its index
map.returns: `list` — as long as the original one.

put.doc: Writes into the list: replaces, inserts, or appends.
params: where to write; `null` means at the end
`'replace'` (the default), `'insert'` to slip it in before the index, `'extend'` to append the elements of another list
examples: list.put(l, null, 4);                 // appends at the end
list.put(l, null, [7, 8], 'extend');  // appends 7 and 8, not the list
put.note: It changes the list in place. When the find argument is already an access (`put(l:0, 9)`), that is container and address together: it writes element `0` of `l`.

range.doc: A lazy list of numbers, from `start` (included) to `end` (excluded).
params: the find value; without it, zero
the increment; without it, one. It can be negative or decimal
range.returns: `list` — lazy: the elements are produced as they are consumed.
range.note: Being lazy, `range(1000000)` allocates nothing, but it also does not know its own size: `size(range(5))` does **not** answer `5`. Materialise it find with `slice(range(5), 0, 5)`.

reduce.doc: Folds a list into a single value, carrying an accumulator through the elements.
params: computed for every element: `_a` is the accumulator, `_` the element, `_i` its index
the starting value of the accumulator
reduce.returns: the accumulator after the last element.
examples: list.reduce(items, _a + _:1, 0);             // the total of the counts

remove.doc: Removes the element at that index, shifting the following ones.
remove.note: Unlike reading, which wraps around, deleting an index that does not exist is an `IndexOutOfBoundsError`: removing something that is not there is always a mistake.

reverse.doc: The list read the other way round.
reverse.returns: `list` — a new reversed list; the original one is untouched.

size.doc: How many elements the list has - and the number of characters, on a string.
size.note: On a lazy list (`range`) it does not answer the real size: materialise it with `slice` find.

slice.doc: A piece of the list, from one index (included) to another (excluded).
params: the index to stop before; without it, to the end
slice.returns: `list` — a new list with the chosen piece.

sort.doc: Sorts a list, by the values or by a key.
params: optional: an expression with `_`, or a function, computing what to sort by
sort.returns: `list` — a new sorted list; the original one is untouched.

get.doc: The value stored under a key, `null` when it is not there - the same thing the `:` operator does.
examples: m:'a';                 // the same thing, without importing

has.doc: Whether the key is in the map.
examples:
// it tells apart an absent key from one holding null
map.has(m, 'k');   // false, while m:'k' is null in both cases

keys.doc: The keys of the map, as a list.

pairs.doc: The map as a list of `[key, value]` pairs.
pairs.returns: `list` — one two element list per entry.
examples:
// sorting a map by value
list.sort_key(map.pairs(scores), -_:1);

put.doc: Writes a value under a key, replacing what was there.
put.returns: the previous value, `null` when the key was not there.
put.note: It changes the map in place. It is atomic even between tasks; a *sequence* of operations is not — for that there is `synchronize` in `core.start`.

remove.doc: Removes a key from the map.
remove.returns: the removed value, `null` when the key was not there.

size.doc: How many entries the map has.

values.doc: The values of the map, as a list.

decode.doc: Reads a json string back as ordinary Blossom values.
decode.returns: the value: a map for an object, a list for an array, and so on.
decode.note: Invalid json is a typed error saying where the problem is, not a `null` to be discovered later. Catch it with `try(..., 'json_error', ...)` when the text comes from outside.

encode.doc: Turns a Blossom value into a json string.
params: maps, lists, numbers, strings, booleans and `null`

count.doc: How many tasks are running right now.
params: optional: only the ones of that group
count.returns: `num` — the number of tasks in flight.
examples:
// waiting for everything to quiet down
while(start.count() > 0, 1000, start.sleep(50));

dock.doc: Runs the expression on the main thread of the game and waits for its result.
params: what to run inside the tick
examples:
// inside a start: the world can only be touched from here
task.dock(block.set([0, 64, 0], 'stone'));
dock.note: Everything in `core.mc.*` needs this when it is called from a start. Keep what goes inside it short: it runs in the tick, and while it runs the server waits.

done.doc: Whether the start has already finished, without waiting for it.

has_next.doc: Whether the start has a value waiting to be read.

next.doc: Waits for the start to finish without asking for its value.
examples: for(tasks, start.next(_));   // waits for all of them

send.doc: Sends a value into a running start, where a `yield` is waiting for it.

sleep.doc: Suspends the current thread for a while.
sleep.note: Inside a start it is fine. On the main thread it stops the server: to wait in the game there is `schedule` in `core.mc.event`, which counts ticks and lets the world go on.

start.doc: Starts a function on another thread and comes back at once with a handle to it.
params: the function to run, passed as a value
start.returns: the handle of the start, to be passed to the other functions of this module.
start.note: The start runs **outside** the tick of the game: to touch blocks, entities or anything else of the world from inside it, wrap that part in `dock`.

synchronize.doc: Runs the expression with a lock held, so two tasks never do it at the same time.
params: the name of the lock, any value; the same name means the same lock
examples:
// read and write are two steps: without the lock a count gets lost
task.synchronize('counter', counter = counter + 1);
synchronize.note: The lock is reentrant (a synchronised function can call another one on the same lock) and fair (whoever waits gets in in the order they arrived). Single operations — an assignment, a `put`, a `remove` — are already atomic on their own and need no lock; it is *sequences* that do.

value.doc: The value of the start when it has one, without waiting.
value.returns: the value produced, or `null` when it is not ready.

wait.doc: Waits for the start to finish and returns its value.
wait.note: It blocks the thread that calls it. Calling it from the tick of the game means stopping the server until the start ends — from there use `wait` of `core.mc.system`, which knows how to wait without blocking the tick.

yield.doc: From inside a start: hands a value out and suspends until somebody asks for the next one.
params: what to hand out; without it, `null`
yield.note: It is what turns a start into a generator: it produces on demand instead of computing everything and holding it in memory.

core.io.doc: files, inside declared roots — NBT and datapacks included

append_text.doc: Adds a string at the end of a file, without reading it find.
params: the name of the root, which has to be writable

create_datapack.doc: Creates a datapack from the given content and turns it on.
params: a map from path to file content, nested
create_datapack.returns: `bool` — whether it was created; `null` when a pack with that name is already there.
create_datapack.note: Turning the pack on reloads the server's resources: a call for the loading of an app, not for something inside `tick`. It is here because a datapack is a tree of files.

delete_file.doc: Deletes a file, or a folder that is **empty**.
params: the name of the root, which has to be writable
delete_file.note: It does not remove trees, on purpose: a recursive deletion behind a short name is the easiest way to lose data to a path that is wrong by one character. It is called `delete_file` and not `remove` because `remove` already removes an element from a list or a map.

exists.doc: Whether a file or a folder is there.
exists.returns: `bool` — whether something exists at that path.

is_directory.doc: Whether that path is a folder rather than a file.

list.doc: The names inside a folder, sorted.
params: the folder to read; `''` is the root itself
list.returns: `list` — the names, without the path in front.
list.note: It is **not** recursive, on purpose: a recursion over a big root blocks the tick without the author noticing. Whoever wants to walk down a tree writes it one level at a time — and while writing it, sees it.

make_directory.doc: Creates a folder, and the intermediate ones it needs.
params: the name of the root, which has to be writable
make_directory.note: The writing functions already create the folders they need: this one is for preparing an empty one.

modified.doc: When the file was last modified.
modified.returns: `num` — milliseconds since the epoch, or `null` when the file is not there.
examples:
age = system.unix_time() - io.modified('shared', 'state.json');
if(age > 60000, send('older than a minute'));

read_json.doc: The content of a file read as json.
read_json.returns: the value: a map, a list, a number, whatever the file holds.

read_lines.doc: The content of a file as a list of lines.
read_lines.returns: `list` — one string per line, without the line breaks.

params: the name of an io root: `'data'` and `'shared'` are always there
the path inside that root, extension included
read_nbt.returns: `nbt` — the compound tag; `null` when the file is not there.
examples:
state = io.read_nbt('data', 'my-app/state.nbt');
if(state == null, state = nbt('{}'));
read_nbt.note: Same roots and same boundaries as every other function here. It is implemented in the Minecraft layer because NBT is a binary format of the game, and it is the one reader that gives back `null` instead of throwing on a missing file.

read_text.doc: The whole content of a file as a single string.

roots.doc: The names of the roots an administrator has declared in `config/blossomscript.json`.
roots.returns: `list` — the names list; empty when nothing is configured.
examples: if(!(io.roots() ~ 'shared'), send('this server has no shared folder'));
roots.note: There are no absolute paths in scripts: every function of this module starts with one of these names, and the rest of the path is relative to it.

size.doc: The size of a file in bytes.
size.returns: `num` — the bytes, or `null` when the file is not there.

writable.doc: Whether that root can be written to, or is read only.

write_json.doc: Writes a value to a file as json.
params: the name of the root, which has to be writable

write_nbt.doc: Writes a compound tag as a compressed NBT file, creating the missing folders.
params: the name of a writable io root
the path inside that root, extension included
write_nbt.note: It needs a compound tag: a list or a bare number is not a valid NBT file, and refusing it at the call beats writing something no reader accepts.

write_text.doc: Writes a string to a file, replacing what was there and creating the missing folders.
params: the name of the root, which has to be writable

encode_query.doc: A map turned into a query string, keys and values encoded.
params: map of parameter name to value
encode_query.returns: `str` — the pairs joined with `&`, sorted so the same map always gives the same string.

encode_url.doc: Percent-encodes one piece of a url.

get.doc: A GET request, giving back the whole response.
params: optional map of header name to value
get.note: A request never runs on the server thread: wrap the call in `start(...)`, or it fails with an error saying so. A status outside 2xx is an answer, not an error.

get_json.doc: A GET asking for json, giving back the body already decoded.
params: optional map of header name to value
get_json.returns: the decoded body, as maps, lists and values.
get_json.note: A body that is not valid json throws `json_error`. The status is not visible here: use `get` when it matters.

hosts.doc: The host patterns an administrator has allowed in `config/blossomscript.json`.
hosts.returns: `list` — the patterns; empty when this server has no network open.
examples: if(size(http.hosts()) == 0, send('no network on this server'));
hosts.note: Nothing is reachable until it is declared. A host is either exact or has one leading wildcard (`*.example.com`, which does not match `example.com` itself).

post.doc: A POST request with the body sent as UTF-8 text.
params: optional map of header name to value

post_json.doc: Sends a value encoded as json and decodes the answer the same way.
params: what to encode as the body
optional map of header name to value
post_json.returns: the decoded body, as maps, lists and values.

request.doc: Any method: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE or HEAD.
params: optional map of header name to value

bool.doc: Reads a value as a truth value, the way a condition would.
bool.returns: `bool` — `false` for `0`, the empty string, an empty list or map, `null`, and for the strings `'false'` and `'null'`.
examples: system.bool('no');      // true: only 'false' and 'null' are special
bool.note: The two special strings are there for values read from a configuration file, where `false` arrives as text and a plain non empty string would be true.

convert_date.doc: Breaks a timestamp into date pieces, and puts them back together the other way round.
params: milliseconds since the epoch, or a list `[year, month, day, hour, minute, second]` to go the other way
convert_date.returns: `list` — `[year, month, day, hour, minute, second, weekday, day_of_year]`, or `num` when given a list.

copy.doc: A deep copy of a value: lists and maps inside it are copied too.
copy.returns: a new value, sharing nothing with the original.
copy.note: Assigning a list does not copy it: the two names point to the same list. This is the way to really have two.

measure.doc: Runs an expression over and over for a fixed interval and says how many times it managed to.
measure.returns: `num` — the number of repetitions in the interval; the higher, the faster.
measure.note: It answers "how long does this piece take", not "who is eating the tick". For the second question there is `/blossom profile start <app>`, which measures function by function with self time and total time.

time.doc: A monotonic counter in milliseconds, with a decimal part - the one to measure durations with.
time.note: It only means something as a difference: the origin is arbitrary. For an absolute date there is `unix_time`.

type.doc: The name of the type of a value.

undef.doc: Removes a variable or a function by name.
params: the name to remove; ending it with `*` removes everything with that prefix
undef.note: A tool for the console and for cleaning up, not for ordinary logic: code removing its own names at runtime cannot be read from the outside.

unix_time.doc: Absolute time in milliseconds since the find of January 1970.

var.doc: Reads (and creates, when it is not there) a variable from its name as a string.
var.returns: the value of the variable, `null` when it did not exist.
var.note: For debugging, not for normal logic: a direct access is clearer and faster, and it is the one the editor can follow.

vars.doc: The names of the visible variables starting with a prefix.
params: the beginning of the name; `'global'` looks among the globals

air.doc: Whether there is air at that point.

blast_resistance.doc: How well the block resists explosions.

block.doc: The block at a position, as a value that compares and prints as its name.
params: the position, as `[x, y, z]` or as three loose arguments
or the name of a block, to build the value without reading the world
block.returns: `block` — printed and compared it is its name, `'minecraft:stone'`.
examples: block.block('oak_stairs[facing=north]');        // from a name, with properties

blocks_daylight.doc: Whether the block stops daylight from going further down.
blocks_daylight.returns: `bool` — true when skylight does not propagate through it.

blocks_movement.doc: Whether the block stops whoever walks into it.

catalog.doc: Every block the game knows, or the ones carrying a tag.
params: optional: only the blocks of that tag

data.doc: The NBT of the block entity - the content of a chest, the text of a sign.
data.returns: `nbt` — the data, `null` when that block has no block entity.

destroy.doc: Breaks the block: with drops, without, or as if a given tool had broken it.
params: `-1` for no drops, or an item such as `'diamond_pickaxe'`; with `[name, count, nbt]` its enchantments count

signatures: explosion(pos, power, type, fire, source, cause)
explosion.doc: Sets off an explosion at a point.
params: optional: the strength, `4` like TNT by default
optional: the entity to blame for the damage

flammable.doc: Whether fire can catch on that block.

hardness.doc: How hard the block is to break.
hardness.returns: `num` — the hardness; `-1` when it cannot be broken, as for bedrock.

harvest.doc: Breaks a block the way that player would break it, with their tool and enchantments.
harvest.note: Unlike `destroy`, it fires the events and the statistics of a real breaking: it counts for the tool durability and for whoever is listening.

light.doc: The light at a point, whole or one layer at a time.
params: optional: total, block, sky, effective, emitted, brightness
examples: block.light([0, 64, 0], 'sky');     // only what comes from the sky

liquid.doc: Whether the block is a liquid - water, lava, or something modded that behaves like one.

map_color.doc: The colour the block shows on a map.
map_color.returns: `str` — the name of the colour on the map.

opacity.doc: How much light the block absorbs.
opacity.returns: `num` — the dampening this block applies to light going through it.

place_item.doc: Uses an item on a block, the way a player clicking on it would.
params: the item to use, as a name or a triple
optional: whether to respect the placement rules of the game
place_item.returns: `bool` — whether the use had an effect.

pos.doc: The position of an entity, with its decimals.
examples: block.set(block.pos(player), 'stone');   // it floors on its own

pos_offset.doc: A position shifted in a direction.
params: optional: how many blocks, one by default
examples:
// the block a face is pointing at, inside an event
block.pos_offset(clicked, face);

power.doc: The redstone signal the block emits.

random_tick.doc: Gives the block one random tick, the kind that grows crops.

see_sky.doc: Whether that point has open sky above it.

set.doc: Places a block, with its properties.
params: the name of the block, or a block value taken from the world
the properties, as pairs or as a single map
set.returns: `block` — the block placed, `null` when nothing changed.
examples:
// copying a block along with its data
block.set(there, block.block(here));
set.note: A property the block does not have is an error, with the right name suggested — not a silent default.

solid.doc: Whether the block is solid - something you can stand on and cannot walk through.
examples: if(block.solid([x, y - 1, z]), send('there is ground here'));

sound.doc: The sound group of the block, the one deciding the noise of steps and breaking.
sound.returns: `str` — the name of the group, as `'stone'` or `'wood'`.

state.doc: The properties of the block as a map, or the value of one of them.
params: optional: the name of a single property
state.returns: `map` of name to value, or the single value; `null` when the property is not there.

suffocates.doc: Whether the block suffocates whoever ends up inside it.

tags.doc: The tags the block belongs to, or whether it belongs to one of them.
params: the position of the block, or a block value
tags.returns: `list` of tags, or `bool` when a tag is given.

tick.doc: Runs the scheduled tick of the block right away.
examples: block.tick(water_pos);   // makes the water flow one step

ticks_randomly.doc: Whether the block gets random ticks - the ones growing crops and spreading grass.

transparent.doc: Whether the block lets light through.
transparent.returns: `bool` — whether it is transparent to light.

update.doc: Forces a block update at that point, as if a neighbour had changed.
examples:
// after a bulk build inside without_updates
for(edges, block.update(_));

without_updates.doc: Runs an expression without letting block updates spread.
params: what to run, usually a build
without_updates.note: Nothing is updated when it ends either: call `update` on the edges if the build has to settle.

add_chunk_ticket.doc: Adds a ticket to keep an area loaded.
params: the kind of ticket, as `'portal'` or `'unknown'`
how many chunks around, from 1 to 32
add_chunk_ticket.note: Tickets expire on their own: this is not a permanent chunk loader, it is a way of holding an area up for a while.

biome.doc: The biome at a point, or a property of a biome by name.
params: or the name of a biome, with the property to ask for: `'temperature'`, `'downfall'`, `'category'`, `'fog_color'`, ...
biome.returns: `str` with the name of the biome, or the value of the property.

chunk_generated.doc: Whether the chunk already exists on disk, without generating it.
params: optional: with `true` it loads it to check
chunk_generated.returns: `bool` — whether the chunk was already created.

chunk_tickets.doc: The tickets keeping chunks loaded, everywhere or at one point.
params: optional: only the tickets of that chunk
chunk_tickets.returns: `list` — one entry per ticket, with type, level and position.

day_time.doc: The time of day, and with an argument the way to set it.
params: optional: the new time in ticks; `0` is dawn, `6000` noon, `18000` midnight
day_time.returns: `num` — the time of day in ticks.

generation_status.doc: How far the generation of that chunk got.
params: optional: with `true` it loads it to check

in_dimension.doc: Runs an expression as if the script were in another dimension.
params: the dimension to move to, or an entity to borrow it from
examples:
// following a player wherever they are
world.in_dimension(player, block.set(block.pos(player), 'stone'));
in_dimension.note: Every function of the game layer inside it looks at that dimension: it is the way to touch the Nether from a script running in the Overworld.

in_slime_chunk.doc: Whether slimes can spawn in that chunk.
in_slime_chunk.returns: `bool` — whether it is a slime chunk.
examples: if(world.in_slime_chunk(pos), send('good spot for a farm'));

inhabited_time.doc: How long players have spent in that chunk, in ticks - what raises the local difficulty.

load_status.doc: How deeply the chunk is loaded.
load_status.returns: `num` — `0` not loaded, growing with the level of loading.

loaded.doc: Whether the chunk holding that point is in memory.

loaded_for_entities.doc: Whether the chunk is loaded deeply enough for entities to be processed in it.

place_feature.doc: Places a feature or a structure of the generator at that point: trees, geysers, villages.
params: the name of the feature or of the structure

poi.doc: The points of interest around a point: beds, work stations, portals.
params: optional: with `true` the nearest come find
optional: only that kind of point
poi.returns: `map` of the single point, or `list` of the points found.

reload_chunk.doc: Sends the chunk to the clients again, without changing anything on the server.
examples: world.reload_chunk(pos);   // fixes a client that shows the wrong blocks

sample_noise.doc: Samples a density function of the world generator, or lists the ones that exist.
params: the name of the density function
sample_noise.returns: `list` of names with no arguments, `num` with them.

save.doc: Forces the world to be written to disk right now.
save.note: It is a heavy operation that runs inside the tick: fine before a risky change, not something to put in a loop.

set_biome.doc: Changes the biome at a point.
params: optional: whether to send the change to the clients, `true` by default
set_biome.note: It changes a whole vertical section of 4x4x4 blocks, not one block: that is the resolution biomes are stored at.

set_poi.doc: Creates a point of interest, or removes the one at that position.
params: its kind, or `null` to remove it
optional: how many free places it has

spawn_potential.doc: The spawn potential the game computes for that point.
spawn_potential.returns: `num` — the potential; the higher, the more crowded the game considers the area.

tick.doc: Forces the server forward by a tick, and with an argument keeps ticking for that long.
params: optional: how long to keep running ticks
tick.note: It is what makes the world move on from inside a script that is itself running inside a tick: without it, a loop waiting for something in the world waits forever.

tick_time.doc: The number of the tick the server is running right now.
tick_time.returns: `num` — the counter of the ticks of the server.
examples:
// doing something every 20 ticks, from inside a tick event
if(world.tick_time() % 20 == 0, work());

top.doc: The find free height at that column, according to one of the height maps.
params: the position; only x and z are used
top.returns: `num` — the y of the find free block.

weather.doc: Reads or sets rain and thunder.
params: `'clear'`, `'rain'`, `'thunder'`; asking without a duration reads how long it has left
optional: how many ticks it lasts
weather.returns: `str` when read with no arguments, `num` of remaining ticks when a type is asked about, `null` when setting.
examples: world.weather('rain', 6000);     // it rains for five minutes

diamond.doc: The positions of an octahedron - everything within a given distance walking along the axes.
params: optional: the distance on the horizontal plane
optional: how far up and down; without it, the shape is a full octahedron
examples:
// a flat disc, height zero
for(scan.diamond(pos, 5, 0), block.set(_, 'stone'));

neighbors.doc: The six positions touching a block by a face.
examples:
// a flood fill starts here
next = list.filter(scan.neighbors(pos), block.air(_));

rect.doc: The positions of a box, as a lazy list.
params: optional: how far on the three axes, one number or a triple
optional: the radii of an inner box to leave out, so only the shell is left
rect.returns: `list` — lazy: the positions come out as they are consumed.
examples:
// only the shell: a box of radius 4 minus the one of radius 3
for(scan.rect(pos, [4, 4, 4], [3, 3, 3]), block.set(_, 'glass'));
rect.note: Being lazy it builds no list in memory: a `rect` of radius 50 costs the same as one of radius 1 until it is consumed.

scan.doc: Walks over a box of blocks around a centre, running an expression at every point.
params: how far to go on the three axes: a triple `[2, 1, 2]` or three loose numbers
optional: with two groups of radii the box can be asymmetric
computed at every point: `_x`, `_y`, `_z` are the coordinates and `_` is the block
scan.returns: `num` — how many times the expression came out true.
examples:
// counting is a single line
ores = scan.scan(pos, 8, 8, 8, _ == 'diamond_ore');

// a flat area: no radius on y
scan.scan(pos, [8, 0, 8], block.set([_x, _y, _z], 'grass_block'));
scan.note: Returning how many times the expression was true is what makes counting free: no accumulator, no `filter` over a materialised list.

volume.doc: Like `scan`, but the box is given with two corners instead of a centre and radii.
volume.returns: `num` — how many times the expression came out true.
volume.note: The order of the corners does not matter: it sorts them itself.

core.mc.entity.doc: finding, creating and modifying entities and players

area.doc: The entities of a type inside a box around a point.
params: the type, `'*'` for all of them
how far on the three axes, one number or a triple

by_id.doc: An entity from its numeric id or from its uuid.
params: the numeric id of the entity, or its uuid as a string
by_id.returns: `entity` — the entity, `null` when it is not loaded.
by_id.note: The numeric id only lives as long as the entity is loaded; the uuid follows it across restarts.

has_client.doc: Whether that player has Blossom installed on the client too.
has_client.returns: `bool` — whether they will see real shapes instead of particles.
has_client.note: It is not needed to draw: `draw` decides on its own, player by player. It is for offering something different to those who have the client.

list.doc: Every entity of a type in the loaded world.
params: a type such as `'zombie'`, `'*'` for all of them, `'!player'` for everything but players
examples: size(entity.list('*'));   // how many entities there are
list.note: It walks over the whole loaded world: on a busy server this is not free, and `area` is almost always the question you actually meant.

modify.doc: Writes an attribute of an entity.
params: what to write; some attributes take several values
modify.returns: the entity, so calls can be chained.

on.doc: Attaches a handler to *that* entity alone.
params: the handler, as a value; `null` removes it
extra arguments, arriving after the ones of the event
examples:
fn watch(e) -> if(entity.query(e, 'y') < 0, entity.modify(e, 'kill'));
entity.on(mob, 'on_tick', watch);
on.note: The handler lives inside the entity: it follows it between worlds and disappears with it. The find argument is always the entity itself, and the number of arguments is checked at once, not at the find event.

on_load.doc: Calls a function every time an entity of one of those types appears in the world.
params: a type, a list of types, or `null` for all of them
on_load.note: The filter by type happens **before** the call: listening for a rare type costs nothing for every other entity appearing in the world. The unfiltered version is the `entity_loads` event in `core.mc.event`.

player.doc: The player running the script, one by name, or the list of those in a category.
params: the name of a player, or a category: `'all'`, `'survival'`, `'creative'`, `'spectating'`, `'!spectating'`
player.returns: `entity` for a single player, `list` for a category, `null` when nobody matches.

query.doc: Reads an attribute of an entity.
query.returns: the value of the attribute, `null` when the entity does not have it.
query.note: `query(entity, 'nbt')` is the way out when a script needs something the curated attributes do not cover.

select.doc: The entities a vanilla selector would pick.

spawn.doc: Creates an entity at a point.
params: optional: the same data a `/summon` would take
spawn.returns: `entity` — the entity created, `null` when it could not be.

types.doc: The registered entity types, or the ones of a category.

catalog.doc: Every item the game knows, or the ones carrying a tag.
params: optional: only the items of that tag

component.doc: A single data component of an item.
params: the id of the component, as `'minecraft:damage'`
optional: with `true` it reads the value of the kind of item
component.returns: the value of the component, `null` when the stack does not carry it.

component_catalog.doc: The ids of every data component this game knows.

components.doc: Every data component of an item, as a map from id to value.
params: optional: with `true` it reads the components the **kind of item** has, not the ones this stack carries
components.returns: `map` — from component id to its value.
components.note: Since 1.20.5 an item is an id plus typed components, not free-form NBT. Reading through the raw NBT still works for what is in the NBT, but it cannot tell an absent value from one equal to the default.

crafting_remainder.doc: What is left in the grid after using that item in a recipe.
crafting_remainder.returns: `str` — the name of what remains, `null` when nothing does.

max_stack.returns: `num` — the maximum size of a stack.

name.doc: The name of the item as the game shows it, translated.
params: the item, as a name or as a triple

recipes.doc: The recipes producing an item: ingredients, result and kind.
recipes.returns: `list` — one entry per recipe, `null` when there is none.

set_component.doc: The item with one component changed, or removed when the value is `null`.
params: the new value; `null` removes the component
set_component.returns: `list` — a **copy** of the item with the change; the original is untouched.
set_component.note: A value that makes no sense for that component is refused right away by the codec, with a `TypeMismatchError` — the alternative is a broken item discovered much later, when somebody tries to use it.

tags.doc: The tags of an item, or whether it carries one of them.
tags.returns: `list` of tags, or `bool` when a tag is given.

core.mc.inventory.doc: inventories, of whoever carries one and of whatever contains one

drop.doc: Throws the content of a slot on the ground.
params: the entity or the position holding it
optional: how many; without it, everything

find.doc: The find slot holding a given item.
params: the entity or the position holding it
the item to look for; `null` finds the find empty slot
find.returns: `num` — the slot, `null` when there is none.
examples: item.find(player, null);            // the find free slot

get.doc: The content of a slot, or of the whole inventory.
params: the entity or the position holding it
optional: which slot; without it, all of them
get.returns: `list` — the item as `[name, count, nbt]`, or the list of every slot; `null` when the slot is empty.
examples:
// counting what is in a chest
list.reduce(item.get(chest_pos), _a + (_ == null ? 0 : _:1), 0);

has.doc: Whether the inventory holds everything asked for.
params: the entity or the position holding it
the items, as names or as `[name, count]` pairs
has.returns: `bool` — whether all of them are there.

remove.doc: Takes items out of an inventory, wherever they are in it.
params: the entity or the position holding it
optional: how many, one by default
remove.returns: `bool` — `true` when everything asked for was taken out.
remove.note: It is all or nothing: with fewer than `count` in the inventory it removes nothing and answers `false`.

set.doc: Writes a slot of an inventory.
params: the entity or the position holding it
optional: the item to put there; without it, only the count changes
optional: the data of the item
set.returns: `list` — what was in the slot before.

size.doc: How many slots an inventory has.
params: an entity carrying it, or the position of a block containing one
size.returns: `num` — the number of slots, `null` when there is no inventory there.

core.mc.structure.doc: structure templates, and the structures of the generator

at.returns: `map` from name to the box it takes up, or the single box; `null` when there is none.

eligibility.doc: Whether a structure *could* be born in that chunk, without generating it.
params: optional: which structure to ask about, `null` for all of them
optional: with `true` it also returns the pieces of the structure
eligibility.returns: `map` or `list` of the eligible at, `null` when there are none.
eligibility.note: It asks the generator, not the world: it answers on chunks nobody has ever visited, without generating them and without loading anything.

signatures: load(name, pos, rotation, mirror, with_entities, integrity, seed)
load.doc: Places a structure template in the world.
params: the minimum corner of the result, whatever the rotation
optional: from `0` to `1`; below `1` it drops random blocks, like the structure block
optional: the seed of that randomness, to make a ruin repeatable
load.returns: `bool` — whether it succeeded, `null` when the template does not exist.
examples:
// a repeatable ruin
structure.load('mine:tower', pos, 0, 'none', true, 0.6, 12345);
load.note: `pos` is always the minimum corner of the **result**: without this correction the same call with a different rotation would land somewhere else. It is also what makes `load` and `matches` reciprocal.

matches.doc: Whether the region between two corners matches a template.
params: optional: the rotation to compare with
optional: the mirroring to compare with
matches.returns: `bool` — whether it matches; `null` when the template does not exist, which is not the same as "does not match".
matches.note: A region of a different size is discarded at once, without reading a single block. A template with several palettes matches when at least one of them does, and `structure_void` blocks do not count, as in vanilla.

place.doc: Generates a structure at that point, or removes its reference.

references.doc: The chunks referring to the at that pass through that point.
references.returns: `map` from name to a list of chunk coordinates, or the single list.

save.doc: Saves a volume of the world as a structure template.
params: the name of the template, as `'mine:tower'`
optional: whether to save the entities too, `false` by default
save.note: They are the **same templates as the vanilla structure block**, in the same place (`<world>/generated/<namespace>/structure/<name>.nbt`): what a script saves opens with a structure block, and the other way round.

size.doc: The size of a template, taking a rotation into account.
size.returns: `list` — `[x, y, z]`, `null` when the template does not exist.
examples:
// the far corner of a placement
structure.size('mine:tower', 90);

core.mc.shape.doc: showing what a script is computing

clear.doc: Forgets the shapes still waiting to be redrawn as particles.
clear.note: It does not remove the ones already sent to a client: those expire on their own when their duration runs out.

draw.doc: Draws a shape in the world for a while - the way to see what a script is computing.
params: how long it stays, in ticks
a map: the geometry of that type plus the common ones — `player`, `color`, `fill`, `line`, `follow`, `snap`, `debug`
draw.returns: `num` — how many players got it as a real shape rather than as particles.
examples:
// a ghost block, to show where a piece will go
shape.draw('block', 100, {'pos' -> pos, 'block' -> 'chest[facing=north]'});
draw.note: Whoever has Blossom on the client sees the real shape; whoever plays vanilla sees the same geometry approximated with particles. You do not have to know which is which. A name the shape does not have is an error with the right one suggested, not a silent default — and a colour hand-written in hexadecimal with the alpha at zero is invisible, which is the mistake people make most.

types.doc: The names of the shapes `draw` accepts.

close.doc: Closes the screen: the player goes back to their own inventory.

open.doc: Opens a screen for a player and hands back something that behaves like an inventory.
params: optional: called as `(screen, player, action, data)` — the actions are `'slot_click'`, `'button_click'`, `'select_recipe'`, `'close'`
open.returns: `screen` — usable as an inventory with the functions of `core.mc.item`.
open.note: Returning a true value from the callback cancels the action.

property.doc: Reads or writes a property of the screen: the level of an enchantment, the progress of a furnace, the fuel.
params: the name of the property, which depends on the type of screen
property.returns: the value of the property, or `bool` when writing.

params: optional: what feeds it, `'dummy'` by default

display.doc: Shows an objective in a display slot, or reads which one is there.
params: optional: the objective to show; `null` clears the slot

property.doc: Reads or writes a property of an objective.
property.returns: the value of the property, or the new one when writing.

remove.doc: Deletes an objective, or removes the score of a single one from it.
params: optional: only their score goes away

score.doc: Reads the objectives, the scores of one, the score of somebody, or writes it.
params: a player, an entity, or any name
score.returns: `list` of objectives, `map` of scores, `num` of a single score, or the previous value when writing.

add.doc: Creates a team, or puts somebody in it.
params: optional: the player or the name to add

leave.doc: Takes somebody out of whatever team they are in.

list.doc: The teams that exist, or the members of one.
params: optional: the team to look inside
list.returns: `list` — the names of the teams, or of the members.

property.doc: Reads or writes a property of a team.

core.mc.bossbar.doc: the bars at the top of the screen

bar.doc: The boss bars that exist, the creation of one, and its properties.
bar.returns: `list` of the bars, the value of the property, or the created bar.

core.mc.nbt.doc: the raw data of the game

decode.doc: The opposite of `nbt`: from NBT to ordinary Blossom values.
params: the NBT value, or its textual form
decode.note: The result is a plain copy: changing it does not change the entity or the block it came from.

params: optional: with `true`, whatever has no NBT shape becomes its string instead of failing

escape.doc: Puts a string in the form the game would write it inside a tag, quotes and escapes included.
examples:
// building a tag by hand without breaking it on an apostrophe
nbt.nbt('{Name: ' + nbt.escape(name) + '}');

matches.doc: Whether a tag satisfies a partial predicate, with the same rules the vanilla commands use.
params: the partial tag it has to contain
optional: whether lists have to match exactly rather than by containment

nbt.doc: Builds an NBT value from a string in command format, from a map or from a list.
params: the text `'{Fire: 20}'`, or a map or list to convert
nbt.returns: `nbt` — indexable like a map or a list, and changeable in place.
nbt.note: It is the way to touch what the curated API does not expose yet: everything the game stores goes through here.

storage.doc: The NBT storage of the world, the one the commands call `data storage`.
storage.returns: `list` of the keys, the stored tag, or the written value.
storage.note: It is the way to exchange data with functions and datapacks: they read the same storage with `/data get storage`.

format.doc: Builds formatted text. Every piece is `'style text'`, where the style is a run of letters.
params: the pieces, in order. Colours: `w` white, `y` yellow, `m` magenta, `r` red, `c` cyan, `l` light green, `t` blue, `f` dark grey, `g` grey, `d` gold, `p` purple, `n` dark red, `q` dark cyan, `e` dark green, `v` dark blue, `k` black, `#rrggbb` exact. Styles: `i` italic, `b` bold, `u` underlined, `s` struck through, `o` obfuscated
format.returns: `text` — formatted text, usable everywhere a message goes.
examples: text.format('rb Warning', 'w  the area is unstable');

// an action attached to the piece before it
text.format('c click here', '!/say hello', '^g runs a command');
format.note: A piece starting with a symbol attaches an action to the piece before it: `^` text on hover, `!` runs a command, `?` writes it in chat, `@` opens an address, `&` copies to the clipboard.

hud.doc: A line of text above the hotbar, which stays there.
params: a player or a list of players
what to show; `null` removes the line
optional, in ticks: **without it the line stays**, there is no hidden default
hud.returns: `num` — how many players were touched; with one argument, the line they are seeing or `null`.
examples: text.hud(player, 'ores found: ' + found);        // stays until you change it
text.hud(player, 'unstable area', 60);           // three seconds, then it goes
hud.note: It works on any client, with nothing installed: it is the action bar, resent before it fades. Three consequences — there is only one line, it shares the space with everything else writing there, and the position is not up for choice. A duration of zero or less is an error, not "disappears at once": whoever writes it has almost always miscomputed an interval.

send.doc: Writes a message in chat: to whoever launched the script, or to a given target.
params: optional: a player, or a **list** of players
send.returns: the message, so the call can be slipped in the middle of an expression.
examples: text.send(player, text.format('rb watch out', 'w  something went wrong'));
send.note: The target takes a list as it is: `entity.player('all')` goes in with no loop around it.

signatures: title(targets, type, text, fade_in, stay, fade_out)
params: a player or a list of players
what to write, plain or formatted
optional: the three times, in ticks

signatures: particle(name, pos, how_many, spread, speed, player)
particle.doc: Spawns particles at a point. With no arguments, the particles that exist.
params: the particle, as `'flame'`; it takes parameters too, `'dust 1 0 0 1'`
optional: how many, one by default
optional: how far around the point they scatter
optional: only that player sees them
particle.returns: `list` of the names with no arguments, `null` otherwise.
examples: effect.particle('dust 1 0 0 1', pos, 10, 0.3, 0, player);   // only for them

particle_box.doc: The twelve edges of a box in particles - the quick way to show the area a script is working on.
params: optional: how many particles per block
optional: only that player sees it
particle_box.note: For something that stays and takes colours there is `draw` in `core.mc.shape`; this one costs nothing and needs no client.

particle_line.doc: A line of particles between two points.
params: optional: how many particles per block
optional: only that player sees it

post.doc: The post-processing shaders of one or more players - what the game calls `/posteffect`.
params: a player or a list of players
post.returns: `num` of the players changed, or `list` of the active effects for `'list'`.
post.note: It goes through the same packet as the vanilla command, so it works on any client and survives a trip out of the world and back. It has no duration: it is removed explicitly.

sound.doc: Plays a sound at a point, for whoever is close enough to hear it. With no arguments, the sounds that exist.
params: optional: also how far it reaches, `1` by default
sound.returns: `list` of the names with no arguments, `num` of the players who heard it otherwise.
examples: effect.sound();   // every sound the game knows

declare.doc: Like `on`, but it also takes a name the game does not know: that becomes an **application event**.
params: the name of the event, of the game or invented
examples:
// this app declares the event by listening to it
event.declare('mine:round_over', on_round_over);
declare.note: An application event exists from the moment the find app listens to it. It is the way two apps talk without either knowing the functions of the other.

describe.doc: The card of an event: how many arguments it takes, whether it can be cancelled, who is listening.

emit.doc: Raises an application event, calling every app listening to it.
params: what to hand to the handlers
emit.returns: `num` — how many apps were listening, `null` when that event does not exist.

list.doc: The names of every event the catalogue holds.

listeners.doc: How many handlers are listening to an event.

off.doc: Removes the handlers of this app: all of them, or only the ones of an event.
params: optional: only the handlers of this event

on.doc: Registers a handler for an event of the game.
params: the name of the event, from the closed catalogue
the handler, passed **as a value**, not as a name in a string
optional: a list of extra arguments, arriving after the ones of the event
optional: the handler fires only for that player
examples:
// only for one player
event.on('player_jumps', on_jump, [], player);
on.note: The number of arguments is checked at registration: a handler with the wrong signature is a load error, not a line in the log three hours later. A handler returning a true value cancels the action, when the event is cancellable. The handlers of an app go away when the app is reloaded.

schedule.doc: Calls a function a number of ticks from now.
params: what to call, as a value
schedule.note: The times are in ticks and not in milliseconds: a script waiting twenty ticks waits the same amount of *game* time even when the server slows down. It is the way to wait without blocking the tick — `sleep` of `core.start` stops the thread.

info.doc: Information about the server and the process it runs in.
params: optional: which piece — memory, threads, version, loaded mods, uptime, worlds, apps; without it, the list keys
info.returns: `list` of the keys, or the value asked for.

logger.doc: Writes a line to the log of the server.
logger.note: It goes to the console and to `latest.log`, where it stays: `send` only reaches whoever is playing right now.

mob_counts.doc: How many mobs of each category are around, and how many the cap would allow.
mob_counts.returns: `map` from category to `[current, cap]`, or the single pair.

run.doc: Runs a vanilla command with the permissions of the app, collecting its outcome instead of printing it in chat.
params: the command, without the leading slash
run.returns: `list` — `[code, output]`: the return code and the lines the command produced.
examples:
result = system.run('data get entity @p Pos');
if(result:0 > 0, send(result:1));
run.note: It is the way out for what the curated API does not cover: everything it does have is faster and says what went wrong.

params: the entry inside the category, as `'minecraft:jump'`
statistic.returns: `num` — the value, `null` when there is no such statistic.
